ACE inhibitors, ARBs and renin inhibitor

Part 1 · Zinc binders, prodrugs, captopril metabolism, ARB pharmacophore, aliskiren · 28 questions

Question 1

Identify this drug.

Answer: A

Explanation

The structure has a sulfhydryl (HS–CH₂–) zinc-binding group, a methyl at X (alanine mimic), and a proline N-ring carrying the essential COOH. It has no phenyl–(CH₂)ₙ group, which the general ACEI template notes is not present in captopril.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Enalaprilat has a carboxylate zinc binder (–CH(COOH)–NH–) and a phenylethyl group.
  • C: Lisinopril has a lysine side chain ((CH₂)₄NH₂) at X and a phenylethyl group.
  • D: Fosinopril has a phosphinate zinc binder and a cyclohexyl-substituted proline.
Question 2

Which structure is lisinopril?

Answer: D

Explanation

Lisinopril is the lysine derivative of enalaprilat: X is n-butylamine (the lysine side chain) instead of methyl, and the zinc-binding carboxylate is a free acid. That free acid is why it is active without being a prodrug.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Enalapril: methyl at X and an ethyl ester (prodrug).
  • B: Enalaprilat: free acid, but X is methyl (alanine), not the lysine side chain.
  • C: A lysine analog that is still esterified. It would need hydrolysis, which is exactly what lisinopril avoids.
Question 3

Identify this ACE inhibitor.

Answer: C

Explanation

Ramipril keeps the enalapril-type side chain (ethyl ester prodrug, phenylethyl, alanine methyl) but its N-ring is a bicyclic cyclopenta-fused pyrrolidine (a fused cyclopentane ring) carrying the COOH. This is an example of a large hydrophobic N-ring that increases potency and alters pharmacokinetics.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Quinapril's N-ring is a tetrahydroisoquinoline (benzene-fused).
  • B: Enalapril's N-ring is plain proline.
  • D: Fosinopril is a phosphinate with a cyclohexyl on proline.
Question 4

Identify this ACE inhibitor.

Answer: B

Explanation

The N-ring is a tetrahydroisoquinoline (proline replaced by a larger, benzene-fused hydrophobic ring) with the COOH. The ethyl ester shows it is a prodrug, and the phenylethyl mimics phenylalanine.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Ramipril's N-ring is fused to a cyclopentane, not a benzene ring.
  • C: Lisinopril has a lysine side chain, a free acid and plain proline.
  • D: Captopril has an SH group and no phenyl group.
Question 5

In this drug, which group binds the zinc of ACE, and what must happen before it can do so?

Answer: C

Explanation

This is fosinopril. Its zinc binder is a phosphorus-containing (phospho) group. The lecture states that esterifying the carboxylate or phospho zinc binder improves oral activity but requires hydrolysis to the acid form for inhibitory action. Here the ester is the boxed acyloxyalkyl (propionyloxy-isobutyl) group on the phosphorus oxygen.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: There is no SH group in fosinopril.
  • B: This describes enalapril, quinapril and ramipril.
  • D: The proline COOH mimics the C-terminal carboxylate. It is not the zinc binder and is not glucuronidated in this file.
Question 6

Which statement about zinc-binding groups in ACE inhibitors is correct?

Answer: A

Explanation

The three zinc-binding moieties are sulfhydryl, carboxylate and phospho. Sulfhydryl shows superior zinc binding, but SH compounds cause skin rash and taste disturbance and can form disulfides (captopril disulfide), which may shorten duration of action.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: SH binds zinc best.
  • C: Fosinopril is exactly that: a phosphinate prodrug.
  • D: The ester must be hydrolyzed back to the acid before it inhibits ACE. It improves oral activity, not direct inhibition.
Question 7

A patient on captopril reports a metallic loss of taste and a new skin rash. The physician switches him to enalapril and both problems resolve. Which structural difference explains this?

Answer: B

Explanation

Skin rash and taste disturbance are attributed to the sulfhydryl group. Enalapril binds zinc through a carboxylate (released after ester hydrolysis), so it has no SH group.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Enalapril keeps the proline COOH, which is essential.
  • C: Lisinopril, not enalapril, has the lysine side chain.
  • D: Enalapril is a prodrug, and that is unrelated to rash and taste.
Question 8

Which modification of captopril would be expected to destroy its ability to inhibit ACE, according to the SAR?

Answer: D

Explanation

The N-ring must contain a carboxylic acid to mimic the C-terminal carboxylate of ACE substrates. In the binding figure, this carboxylate forms an ionic bond with a positively charged guanidinium group in the active site. The correct analog replaces the COOH with a methyl, which removes that interaction.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Captopril itself, which is active.
  • B: Enalaprilat, an active diacid.
  • C: Lisinopril, which is active without being a prodrug.
Question 9

In the ACE active-site figure, captopril binds through three interactions. Which pairing is correct?

Answer: B

Explanation

The figure shows captopril's SH coordinating Zn²⁺ in place of the scissile carbonyl of angiotensin I. The amide carbonyl hydrogen-bonds to H–X, and the terminal carboxylate binds the positively charged guanidinium (HN–C(=NH₂⁺)–NH). This mirrors how the C-terminus of angiotensin I binds.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: This swaps the roles of the SH and the carboxylate.
  • C: The methyl does not coordinate zinc.
  • D: The proline ring does not bind zinc.
Question 10

In enalapril and quinapril, the boxed phenylethyl group (circled on the slide) is thought to mimic which feature of ACE substrates?

Answer: A

Explanation

The slide labels the phenyl group as mimicking the phenylalanine side chain of the ACE substrate. This group is part of the Ph–(CH₂)ₙ portion of the general template, which captopril lacks.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: The X = methyl group mimics alanine.
  • C: Lysine is mimicked by X = n-butylamine in lisinopril.
  • D: The N-ring COOH mimics the C-terminal carboxylate.
Question 11

In the general ACE inhibitor template, the X group is usually methyl. What does it mimic, and what happens when X is replaced with n-butylamine?

Answer: C

Explanation

X = methyl mimics the side chain of alanine. Within the dicarboxylate series, X = n-butylamine (lysine side chain) produces a compound that is orally active without being a prodrug, as in lisinopril.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Phenylalanine is mimicked by the phenylethyl group, and lisinopril is not a prodrug.
  • B: The lysine analog is active.
  • D: Histidine mimicry is an ARB concept, and taste disturbance is linked to SH.
Question 12

Which ACE inhibitors in this file are not prodrugs?

Answer: D

Explanation

The lecture states that all drugs in the class are prodrugs except captopril and lisinopril. Captopril binds zinc through a free SH group, and lisinopril has a free carboxylic acid.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Enalapril is the ethyl ester prodrug of enalaprilat.
  • B: Ramipril is an ethyl ester prodrug.
  • C: Both are ester prodrugs (fosinopril on its phospho group, quinapril on its carboxylate).
Question 13

Which stereochemical rule does the lecture give for ACE inhibitors?

Answer: A

Explanation

Optimum activity is observed when the inhibitor's stereochemistry matches L-amino acid stereochemistry, which makes sense because the inhibitors mimic peptide substrates.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: This is the opposite.
  • C: The lecture states a specific requirement.
  • D: No such rule is given, and L-proline is the natural configuration.
Question 14

Compared with enalapril (proline N-ring), why might quinapril, ramipril and fosinopril show different potency and pharmacokinetics?

Answer: D

Explanation

Large hydrophobic heterocyclic rings in the N-ring position increase potency and alter pharmacokinetic parameters. Quinapril has a tetrahydroisoquinoline, ramipril a bicyclic ring, and fosinopril a cyclohexyl-substituted proline.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Only captopril has an SH group.
  • B: All of them keep the essential COOH.
  • C: All three are prodrugs.
Question 15

What is this compound, and what is its clinical significance?

Answer: C

Explanation

Two captopril molecules joined through an S–S bond form captopril disulfide. Sulfhydryl-containing compounds can form disulfides, which may shorten duration of action. In the metabolism figure this is shown as dimerization.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: A glutathione conjugate contains the γ-Glu–Cys–Gly tripeptide.
  • B: Lisinopril has no SH group, so it cannot form disulfides.
  • D: Enalaprilat has no sulfur.
Question 16

Which metabolic reaction of captopril produced this metabolite?

Answer: B

Explanation

The SH group has become an S–CH₃ thioether. In the captopril metabolism scheme, this is S-methylation. All four captopril pathways in the file act on the sulfhydryl.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Dimerization gives an S–S-linked dimer of two captopril molecules.
  • C: Cysteine conjugation attaches cysteine through a disulfide.
  • D: Glutathione conjugation attaches the tripeptide γ-Glu–Cys–Gly through a disulfide.
Question 17

Identify the reaction that produced this captopril metabolite.

Answer: A

Explanation

The captopril sulfur is joined by a disulfide to a cysteine that is part of a tripeptide: a γ-glutamyl unit on its NH and a glycine on its carbonyl. That tripeptide is glutathione.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: S-methylation gives S–CH₃, not a disulfide.
  • C: A cysteine conjugate has only cysteine (free NH₂ and COOH), with no glutamyl or glycine units.
  • D: Captopril has no ester to hydrolyze.
Question 18

Which group in all four captopril metabolites shown in the file is the site of metabolism?

Answer: B

Explanation

Dimerization, S-methylation, cysteine conjugation and glutathione conjugation all occur at the SH group. The same group gives captopril its superior zinc binding and its rash and taste side effects.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: The COOH is unchanged in all four metabolites.
  • C: The amide is intact.
  • D: The methyl is unchanged.
Question 19

Identify this drug.

Answer: C

Explanation

It has an imidazole (histidine mimic) carrying an n-butyl chain, Cl and CH₂OH, and a biphenyl with an ortho tetrazole as the acidic group. That is losartan.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Valsartan has no imidazole. It has an acylated valine with an amide bond.
  • B: Candesartan has a benzimidazole with ethoxy and COOH groups.
  • D: Telmisartan has a bis-benzimidazole and an ortho COOH instead of a tetrazole.
Question 20

Which structure is telmisartan?

Answer: D

Explanation

Telmisartan replaces the losartan imidazole and n-butyl with a substituted benzimidazole system (here a bis-benzimidazole), and uses an ortho carboxylic acid on the biphenyl instead of a tetrazole.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Candesartan: a benzimidazole with OEt and COOH, plus a tetrazole on the biphenyl.
  • B: Valsartan: an acylated valine, no heterocycle on the left side.
  • C: Losartan: an imidazole with n-butyl, Cl and CH₂OH.
Question 21

Identify this drug and the part that replaces losartan's imidazole.

Answer: C

Explanation

This is valsartan: an N-pentanoyl (valeryl) valine attached to the biphenyl tetrazole. The imidazole, or an isosteric equivalent, is required to mimic the histidine side chain of angiotensin II. In valsartan, the amide bond plays that role.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: No benzimidazole is present.
  • B: This is not losartan, and the valine COOH is an acidic group, not the histidine mimic.
  • D: Telmisartan uses a COOH, not a tetrazole, and this structure is not telmisartan.
Question 22

Identify this ARB.

Answer: B

Explanation

The n-butyl/imidazole of losartan is replaced by a benzimidazole carrying an ethoxy group and a COOH, while the biphenyl keeps the ortho tetrazole. That is candesartan as drawn in the file.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Telmisartan has a bis-benzimidazole and a biphenyl COOH, not a tetrazole.
  • C: Losartan has an imidazole with n-butyl.
  • D: Valsartan has no ring system on the amide side.
Question 23

Based on the ARB SAR, which analog is expected to be the most active?

Answer: A

Explanation

In the biphenyl series, the tetrazole (or carboxylate) must be in the ortho position for optimal activity. The acidic group is essential, so removing it destroys activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Tetrazole moved to meta: suboptimal.
  • C: Tetrazole moved to para: suboptimal.
  • D: No acidic group at all. The acidic group is essential for activity.
Question 24

The acidic group of ARBs is essential. What is it thought to mimic, and why is tetrazole generally preferred over carboxylate?

Answer: D

Explanation

The acidic group mimics either the tyrosine phenol or the COOH of aspartic acid in angiotensin II. It can be –COOH, phenyl tetrazole or phenyl carboxylate, and the tetrazole is superior for metabolic stability, lipophilicity and oral bioavailability.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Histidine is mimicked by the imidazole.
  • B: Isoleucine is mimicked by the n-butyl group, and ARBs do not bind zinc.
  • C: This mixes in unrelated concepts.
Question 25

Match each part of losartan to what it mimics in angiotensin II.

Answer: D

Explanation

The n-butyl group provides hydrophobic binding and most likely mimics the isoleucine side chain. The imidazole mimics histidine. The acidic group mimics the tyrosine phenol or aspartate COOH.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: The first two are swapped.
  • B: Phenylalanine mimicry is an ACE inhibitor concept.
  • C: Alanine and lysine mimicry belong to the ACE inhibitor X group.
Question 26

Candesartan and telmisartan differ from losartan in which way described by the SAR?

Answer: C

Explanation

The lecture states that the n-butyl group can be replaced with a substituted benzimidazole ring, as in candesartan and telmisartan.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Both keep an acidic group (candesartan a tetrazole, telmisartan a COOH).
  • B: Both keep the ortho position.
  • D: ARBs do not bind zinc.
Question 27

Identify this drug and its class.

Answer: B

Explanation

This is aliskiren: a peptide-like chain with an amine, a hydroxyl, isopropyl branches, a terminal carboxamide and a dimethoxy-substituted aryl ether. Its distinct peptide appearance is why it acts as a peptidomimetic. It works directly on renin, earlier in the cascade than ACE inhibitors and ARBs.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Valsartan has a biphenyl tetrazole.
  • C: Fosinopril has a phosphinate and proline.
  • D: Lisinopril has a proline and a phenylethyl group.
Question 28

Which statement correctly contrasts aliskiren with ACE inhibitors and ARBs?

Answer: A

Explanation

ACE inhibitors and ARBs work during the later stages of the renin–angiotensin system. Aliskiren works directly on the enzyme renin, a relatively new approach.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: That is how ARBs work.
  • C: That is how ACE inhibitors work.
  • D: Aliskiren is a peptidomimetic, not a biphenyl tetrazole.

β-blockers

Part 2a · From isoprenaline to propranolol, aryloxypropanolamine SAR, β₁ selectivity, metabolism · 25 questions

Question 29

In the development of β-blockers, the phenolic OH groups of (R)-isoprenaline were replaced by chlorine atoms to give dichloroisoprenaline. What was the result?

Answer: B

Explanation

The phenolic groups are important for agonist activity. Replacing them with Cl gave dichloroisoprenaline, a partial agonist. Because it blocks the natural messenger from binding and lowers adrenergic activity, it can be viewed as an antagonist.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Dichloroisoprenaline still had partial agonist activity.
  • C: Removing the phenols reduced agonist activity.
  • D: It acts at β-receptors.
Question 30

Identify this compound and its place in β-blocker development.

Answer: C

Explanation

The aryl group is a 2-naphthyl attached directly to the ethanolamine (no OCH₂ linker). This is pronethalol, made to remove partial agonist activity. It was the first β-blocker used clinically for angina, arrhythmia and high blood pressure, but it was still a partial agonist.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Propranolol has an OCH₂ linker at the 1-position of naphthalene.
  • B: Dichloroisoprenaline has a 3,4-dichlorophenyl ring.
  • D: Isoprenaline has a catechol (3,4-diOH).
Question 31

Which structure is propranolol?

Answer: D

Explanation

Propranolol has an O–CH₂ linking group between the naphthalene and the ethanolamine, with the chain at the 1-position of the naphthalene ring rather than the 2-position. It has a secondary isopropylamine. It was a pure antagonist with 10–20 times the activity of pronethalol.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Pronethalol: no OCH₂ linker, 2-naphthyl.
  • B: Linker present, but at the naphthalene 2-position.
  • C: Tertiary amine. The amine must be secondary.
Question 32

Which statement about propranolol compared with pronethalol is correct?

Answer: A

Explanation

Introducing an oxymethylene (OCH₂) linking group between the naphthalene (1-position) and the ethanolamine gave propranolol, a pure antagonist with 10–20 times the activity of pronethalol.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Partial agonism was the problem being removed.
  • C: The OH is essential and is present.
  • D: Catechol rings are agonist features.
Question 33

In the aryloxypropanolamine pharmacophore, which statement about the side-chain OH is correct?

Answer: D

Explanation

The OH is essential: it forms a high-affinity hydrogen bond with the receptor's Asn. The S-enantiomer is required for this hydrogen bonding.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Removing it would lose the essential hydrogen bond.
  • B: The ionic interaction belongs to the protonated secondary amine.
  • C: The S-enantiomer is required for aryloxypropanolamines.
Question 34

Which modification of propranolol is most likely to retain activity, according to the SAR?

Answer: C

Explanation

The ether oxygen hydrogen-bonds to the receptor. Replacing it with S, CH₂ or NMe is detrimental, while replacing it with NH may be possible (NH can still take part in hydrogen bonding).

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: S replacement is detrimental.
  • B: CH₂ replacement is detrimental.
  • D: NMe replacement is detrimental.
Question 35

A chemist adds a methyl group to one of the side-chain carbons of propranolol (between the ether O and the amine). What is the expected effect?

Answer: B

Explanation

The SAR figure states that substitution on the propanolamine side chain carbons lowers activity but increases metabolic stability.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: This is the reverse.
  • C: The lecture describes effects on both.
  • D: No such effect is described.
Question 36

Why is this propranolol analog expected to be much less active?

Answer: A

Explanation

The nitrogen carries both a methyl and an isopropyl group, so it is tertiary. The amine is involved in an essential ionic bonding interaction and must be secondary.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: The chain is at the 1-position in this structure.
  • C: The OH is present.
  • D: The ether O is present.
Question 37

What role does the bulky N-substituent (isopropyl or tert-butyl) play in aryloxypropanolamine β-blockers?

Answer: A

Explanation

A bulky R₁ on the nitrogen is required for β-selectivity (vs α). Branching and extension of this group are both beneficial because it fits a hydrophobic pocket.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: β₁ selectivity comes from para hydrogen-bonding groups on the aryl ring (and, in third-generation drugs, an extended N-substituent with a hydrogen-bonding group).
  • C: That is the role of R₂ (the aryl ring substituent).
  • D: In the file, glucuronidation occurs at the side-chain OH.
Question 38

According to the pharmacophore slide, what does the R₂ (aryl ring substituent) determine?

Answer: B

Explanation

R₂ determines whether the β-antagonist is hydrophobic or hydrophilic, which influences adverse effects (CNS penetration) and metabolic stability. Para, or ortho plus para, substitution patterns lead to β₁ selectivity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: That is the bulky N-substituent (R₁).
  • C: Stereochemistry is at the side-chain carbinol carbon.
  • D: That is the secondary amine.
Question 39

Identify this β-blocker and the structural feature that gives it a special property.

Answer: D

Explanation

The naphthalene of propranolol is replaced by an indole. This is (S)-pindolol. The pharmacophore slide states that the indole provides intrinsic sympathomimetic activity and decreases the risk of bronchoconstriction.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Timolol has a morpholine–thiadiazole and a tert-butyl group.
  • B: Carvedilol has a tricyclic carbazole and an extended N-substituent.
  • C: Nadolol has a tetrahydronaphthalene diol.
Question 40

Identify this β-blocker.

Answer: C

Explanation

The aromatic part is a 1,2,5-thiadiazole carrying a morpholine, and the amine carries a tert-butyl group. That is (S)-timolol, an example of replacing propranolol's naphthalene with heterocyclic rings.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Pindolol has an indole.
  • B: Oxprenolol has an ortho-allyloxy phenyl.
  • D: Nadolol has a tetrahydronaphthalene diol.
Question 41

A 40-year-old with hypertension taking propranolol complains of vivid nightmares and daytime sedation. Which β-blocker shown here is least likely to cause these effects?

Answer: B

Explanation

CNS effects (dizziness, nightmares, sedation) are typical of lipophilic β-blockers that cross the blood–brain barrier: propranolol, pindolol and oxprenolol. Nadolol is more water-soluble (note the two ring hydroxyls on its tetrahydronaphthalene) and is less likely to cause them.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Oxprenolol is lipophilic and crosses the BBB.
  • C: Pindolol is lipophilic and crosses the BBB.
  • D: Propranolol is the drug causing the problem.
Question 42

A patient with asthma has bronchospasm after starting a β-blocker. Based on the file, which statement explains this?

Answer: D

Explanation

First-generation (nonselective) β-blockers inhibit all β-receptors and can induce asthma. Second-generation drugs are β₁-selective.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Second-generation drugs are β₁-selective, not β₂.
  • B: Para hydrogen-bonding groups give β₁ selectivity.
  • C: The S-enantiomer is needed for activity, not for tissue selectivity.
Question 43

Which compound is expected to show the greatest β₁-selectivity?

Answer: A

Explanation

For β₁ selectivity, the amido group should be in the para position, not ortho or meta. The para amide makes an extra hydrogen bond with the β₁-receptor that does not occur with β₂ (the docking figure shows the para NHCOCH₃ reaching H–X, while the meta isomer cannot).

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Ortho amide: no extra β₁ hydrogen bond.
  • C: Meta amide: shown in the figure missing the extra hydrogen bond.
  • D: No hydrogen-bonding group on the ring.
Question 44

Identify this second-generation β-blocker.

Answer: C

Explanation

A para CH₂CONH₂ (acetamide) on the phenoxy ring with an isopropylamine is (S)-atenolol. The para hydrogen-bonding amide gives β₁ selectivity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Metoprolol has para CH₂CH₂OMe.
  • B: Betaxolol has para CH₂CH₂OCH₂-cyclopropyl.
  • D: Acebutolol has para NHCOⁿPr plus an ortho acetyl.
Question 45

Which structure is acebutolol?

Answer: D

Explanation

Acebutolol has a para butyramide (NHCOⁿPr) and an ortho acetyl group. This is an ortho plus para pattern, which the pharmacophore slide also links to β₁ selectivity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Atenolol: para CH₂CONH₂ only.
  • B: Betaxolol: para cyclopropylmethoxyethyl.
  • C: Metoprolol: para methoxyethyl.
Question 46

Identify this β-blocker.

Answer: B

Explanation

The para substituent is CH₂CH₂O–CH₂–cyclopropyl. That is (S)-betaxolol. Metoprolol is the same structure with a simple methyl ether (CH₂CH₂OMe).

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Metoprolol has CH₂CH₂OCH₃, with no cyclopropyl.
  • C: Oxprenolol has an ortho-allyloxy group.
  • D: Atenolol has CH₂CONH₂.
Question 47

Identify this drug and its generation.

Answer: C

Explanation

The aryl part is a tricyclic carbazole, and the nitrogen carries an extended 2-(2-methoxyphenoxy)ethyl group. This is carvedilol, a third-generation β-blocker. The extended N-substituent includes a hydrogen-bonding group for an extra interaction with the β₁-adrenoceptor, and carvedilol also has α-blocking activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Labetalol is an arylethanolamine with a salicylamide ring and has no carbazole.
  • B: Pindolol has a bicyclic indole and an isopropyl amine.
  • D: Propranolol has a naphthalene and an isopropyl amine.
Question 48

Look at this third-generation drug. How does its backbone differ from the aryloxypropanolamines such as propranolol?

Answer: A

Explanation

This is labetalol. Its ring (a salicylamide: OH ortho to CONH₂) is bonded directly to the CH(OH), like isoprenaline, rather than through O–CH₂. Its extended N-substituent (1-methyl-3-phenylpropyl) places it with carvedilol among drugs that also have α-blocking activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: The amine is secondary.
  • C: The OH is present.
  • D: The ring is a substituted benzene.
Question 49

Which metabolite of propranolol is shown, and what reaction formed it?

Answer: B

Explanation

The isopropyl group has been removed, leaving a primary amine (–NH₂). This is desisopropylpropranolol (DIP), formed by N-dealkylation. This is the side-chain oxidative pathway.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: 4′-OHP keeps the isopropylamine and has an OH para to the ether on the naphthalene.
  • C: 5′-OHP has an OH on the other naphthalene ring.
  • D: The glucuronide carries a glucuronic acid attached to the side-chain oxygen.
Question 50

Identify this propranolol metabolite.

Answer: C

Explanation

The new OH is on the same ring as the ether, para to it (position 4). Propranolol's oxidative pathways involve naphthalene ring hydroxylation at positions 4, 5 and 7, plus side-chain oxidation.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: 5′-OHP has the OH on the other (distal) naphthalene ring.
  • B: DIP has lost the isopropyl group.
  • D: The glucuronide is a conjugate, not a ring hydroxylation.
Question 51

In the metoprolol metabolism scheme, what reaction converts metoprolol into this metabolite (pathway B)?

Answer: A

Explanation

The OH appears on the carbon directly attached to the benzene ring (the benzylic, α-carbon of the methoxyethyl side chain), giving α-hydroxymetoprolol. The methyl ether and the amine are unchanged.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: O-Demethylation would turn the OCH₃ into an OH.
  • C: The isopropylamine is intact.
  • D: The ring itself carries no new OH.
Question 52

In pathway C of metoprolol metabolism, metoprolol gives O-demethylmetoprolol, which then gives this inactive metabolite. What are the two reactions in order?

Answer: D

Explanation

First, O-demethylation converts CH₂CH₂OCH₃ to CH₂CH₂OH (O-demethylmetoprolol). Then the primary alcohol is oxidized to CH₂COOH, giving acid metabolite 2, which is inactive.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: The amine is intact.
  • B: There is no ester in metoprolol.
  • C: No ring hydroxylation or sulfation is shown.
Question 53

Why is this metoprolol metabolite (acid metabolite 1, pathway A) inactive?

Answer: C

Explanation

The secondary amine is gone and the chain now ends in COOH. Per the propranolol SAR, the secondary amine provides an essential ionic bonding interaction, so its loss explains the inactivity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: The side-chain OH is still present.
  • B: The OCH₃ is intact in this metabolite.
  • D: No glucuronic acid is attached.

Calcium channel blockers

Part 2b · 1,4-Dihydropyridine SAR, verapamil and diltiazem metabolism · 21 questions

Question 54

Identify this calcium channel blocker.

Answer: B

Explanation

Symmetric dimethyl esters at C3 and C5, methyls at C2 and C6, and an ortho-nitrophenyl at C4 of a 1,4-dihydropyridine. That is nifedipine.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Nitrendipine has a meta-NO₂ and mixed methyl/ethyl esters.
  • C: Felodipine has a 2,3-dichlorophenyl.
  • D: Isradipine has a benzoxadiazole at C4.
Question 55

Which structure is amlodipine?

Answer: A

Explanation

Amlodipine has an ortho-chlorophenyl at C4, mixed methyl/ethyl esters, and a distinctive 2-aminoethoxymethyl side chain at C2 in place of one ring methyl.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Felodipine: 2,3-dichlorophenyl and ring methyls at C2 and C6.
  • C: Nitrendipine: meta-nitrophenyl.
  • D: Nifedipine: ortho-nitrophenyl and symmetric dimethyl esters.
Question 56

Identify this dihydropyridine.

Answer: D

Explanation

The C4 aryl is a 2,3-dichlorophenyl (ortho and meta Cl), with methyl/ethyl esters and plain C2/C6 methyls. That is felodipine.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Amlodipine has one ortho-Cl and an aminoethoxymethyl side chain.
  • B: Nifedipine has ortho-NO₂.
  • C: Nitrendipine has meta-NO₂.
Question 57

Identify this drug and the ring at C4.

Answer: B

Explanation

The C4 substituent is a fused benzo[1,2,5]oxadiazole (benzofurazan), with an isopropyl ester at one position and a methyl ester at the other. That is isradipine.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: No nitro group is present.
  • C: No chlorine is present.
  • D: No chlorine or aminoethoxy chain is present.
Question 58

Nifedipine is metabolized by CYP3A4 to this product. What is the reaction, and what happens to activity?

Answer: D

Explanation

The 1,4-dihydropyridine has become an aromatic pyridine (the N–H and C4–H are lost). The 1,4-dihydropyridine ring is essential, so the oxidized analog is inactive.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: A piperidine is the fully reduced (saturated) ring, and that product is also inactive.
  • B: Nifedipine has no N-methyl group.
  • C: Both esters are intact.
Question 59

Which analog is expected to retain L-type calcium channel blocking activity?

Answer: C

Explanation

The 1,4-dihydropyridine ring is essential. Substitution at N1, reduction to a piperidine, or oxidation to a pyridine greatly decreases or abolishes activity. Only nifedipine keeps the intact N1–H dihydropyridine.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: N1-methyl: N1 substitution abolishes activity.
  • B: Piperidine (reduced): inactive.
  • D: Pyridine (oxidized): inactive.
Question 60

In the binding-pocket figure, nifedipine's N1–H hydrogen-bonds to a serine and one ester carbonyl hydrogen-bonds to a glutamine. Which SAR rule does this figure best explain?

Answer: A

Explanation

The figure shows the N1–H donating a hydrogen bond to Ser1011 and an ester C=O accepting one from Gln939. Substituting N1 removes the donor, and replacing the esters removes the acceptor. This fits both rules.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: The figure does not address phenyl substitution pattern.
  • C: Toxicity is not shown by the binding figure.
  • D: Electron-donating groups do show good activity.
Question 61

Which C4 analog of nifedipine would be expected to show decreased activity?

Answer: D

Explanation

A substituted phenyl at C4 optimizes activity, while C4 substitution with a small nonplanar alkyl or cycloalkyl group decreases activity. The correct analog has a cyclohexyl at C4.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Meta-nitrophenyl: optimal (meta substitution).
  • B: Nitrendipine: meta-nitrophenyl.
  • C: Felodipine: ortho/meta dichlorophenyl.
Question 62

Which nifedipine analog is expected to retain optimal activity?

Answer: B

Explanation

Ortho or meta substitution of the C4 phenyl gives optimal activity. Unsubstituted or para-substituted rings show a significant decrease. The correct analog has a meta-NO₂.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Para-NO₂: significant decrease.
  • C: Unsubstituted phenyl: significant decrease.
  • D: Cyclohexyl at C4: decreased activity.
Question 63

A student proposes that the nitro group in nifedipine is essential because it is electron-withdrawing. Using the SAR, which analog would best disprove this?

Answer: A

Explanation

Phenyl substitution matters for size and position rather than electronic nature. Both electron-withdrawing ortho/meta substituents and electron-donating groups show good activity. A meta-methoxy (electron-donating) analog that is still active would disprove the claim.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Para-NO₂ is still electron-withdrawing and is inactive because of its position.
  • C: Unsubstituted phenyl is inactive because it lacks an ortho/meta substituent.
  • D: The oxidized pyridine is inactive for a different reason.
Question 64

What is expected if both C3/C5 esters of nifedipine are replaced with nitrile (–C≡N) groups?

Answer: C

Explanation

Ester groups at C3 and C5 optimize activity. Other electron-withdrawing groups show decreased antagonist activity and may even show agonist activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Esters are optimal.
  • B: The lecture specifically says other EWGs are worse.
  • D: The 1,4-DHP scaffold is unchanged.
Question 65

Which DHP in this file has identical esters at C3 and C5?

Answer: B

Explanation

Nifedipine has two methyl esters. Nitrendipine, felodipine and amlodipine have methyl/ethyl esters, and isradipine has methyl/isopropyl.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Methyl and ethyl.
  • C: Methyl and isopropyl.
  • D: Methyl and ethyl.
Question 66

Why are heteroaromatic rings such as pyridine not used at C4 of 1,4-dihydropyridines, according to the lecture?

Answer: D

Explanation

Heteroaromatic rings (pyridine) at C4 give similar therapeutic effects but are not used due to observed animal toxicity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Activity is similar.
  • B: Agonist activity is linked to non-ester EWGs at C3/C5.
  • C: This is not stated.
Question 67

Identify this drug and its structural requirements.

Answer: C

Explanation

Two dimethoxyphenyl rings, a tertiary N-methyl amine, and a quaternary carbon bearing an isopropyl, a nitrile and an aryl ring. That is verapamil, a phenylalkylamine CCB. Its listed requirements are a benzene ring, a tertiary (3°) amino nitrogen and an isopropyl-substituted benzyl ring.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Diltiazem contains a sulfur-containing seven-membered ring.
  • B: Norverapamil has an N–H (secondary amine).
  • D: No dihydropyridine is present.
Question 68

Which reaction converts verapamil into this metabolite, and how active is it?

Answer: A

Explanation

The N–CH₃ has become N–H. This is norverapamil, the principal metabolite formed by N-demethylation, and it retains about 20% of verapamil's activity. Losing the tertiary amine (a structural requirement) fits the reduced activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: All four OCH₃ groups are intact.
  • C: N-Dealkylation removes the whole dimethoxyphenethyl arm.
  • D: Verapamil has no hydrolyzable ester.
Question 69

This metabolite is formed from norverapamil. Name the reaction and its activity.

Answer: C

Explanation

The whole 3,4-dimethoxyphenethyl group has been removed from the nitrogen, leaving a primary amine (–CH₂NH₂). This is N-dealkylation, and the product is inactive.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: N-Demethylation removes only a methyl.
  • B: All OCH₃ groups remain, and verapamil O-demethylation products are inactive.
  • D: No glucuronic acid is attached.
Question 70

This verapamil metabolite has one aromatic OCH₃ converted to OH. What is the reaction, and what is its activity?

Answer: D

Explanation

Converting an aryl OCH₃ to OH is O-demethylation. The lecture states that verapamil O-demethylation produces inactive metabolites (three different O-demethylated products are shown).

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: No new carbon was hydroxylated. A methyl was removed from oxygen.
  • B: The N-methyl is intact.
  • C: Verapamil has no ester.
Question 71

Which metabolite of diltiazem is shown, and what is its activity?

Answer: A

Explanation

The acetate ester at C3 has been hydrolyzed to a free OH. This is deacetyldiltiazem, which is active with about 40–50% of the parent compound's potency.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: The NMe₂ is intact.
  • C: The para-OCH₃ is intact.
  • D: No sulfoxide is formed in the file.
Question 72

Identify the diltiazem metabolic reaction that gave this product.

Answer: B

Explanation

The dimethylaminoethyl group (–CH₂CH₂N(CH₃)₂) has become a methylaminoethyl group (–CH₂CH₂NHCH₃). One N-methyl was removed, which is N-demethylation. The acetate and the aryl OCH₃ are intact.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: The acetate ester is intact.
  • C: The para-OCH₃ is intact.
  • D: Only a methyl, not the whole side chain, was removed.
Question 73

Rank these metabolites by how much of the parent drug's activity they retain, from highest to lowest.

Answer: D

Explanation

Deacetyldiltiazem keeps about 40–50% of the parent's potency, norverapamil about 20%, and the pyridine (oxidized) analog of nifedipine is inactive.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Norverapamil (20%) is less active than deacetyldiltiazem (40–50%).
  • B: Oxidized nifedipine is inactive.
  • C: Two of the three are active.
Question 74

Which structure is diltiazem?

Answer: A

Explanation

Diltiazem has the fused benzene/sulfur seven-membered ring with a lactam N carrying CH₂CH₂N(CH₃)₂, a 3-acetoxy group and a 4-methoxyphenyl.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Deacetyldiltiazem: free OH instead of the acetate.
  • C: O-Desmethyldiltiazem: phenol instead of the methoxy.
  • D: Verapamil: a phenylalkylamine.

Diuretics

Part 3 · Sulfamoylbenzoic acids, torsemide, thiazide chemistry and SAR, thiazide-like drugs · 23 questions

Question 75

Which pairing of a chemical class with its drug(s) is correct, according to the classification?

Answer: B

Explanation

Site-2 (high-efficacy) diuretics are: 5-sulfamoyl-2-aminobenzoic acids (furosemide, azosemide), 5-sulfamoyl-3-aminobenzoic acids (bumetanide, piretanide), and 4-amino-3-pyridinesulfonylureas (torsemide). Site-3 (medium efficacy) are the thiazides and thiazide-like drugs.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Furosemide and azosemide are 2-aminobenzoic acids.
  • C: Bumetanide and piretanide are 3-aminobenzoic acids.
  • D: Both are site-2 (high efficacy) diuretics.
Question 76

Identify this drug.

Answer: C

Explanation

COOH at C1, a furfurylamino at C2, Cl at C4 and SO₂NH₂ at C5. That is furosemide, the anthranilic acid (5-sulfamoyl-2-aminobenzoic acid) prototype.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Azosemide has a tetrazole at C1 and a thienylmethyl amine.
  • B: Bumetanide has a butylamino at C3 and a phenoxy at C4.
  • D: Piretanide has a pyrrolidine at C3 and a phenoxy at C4.
Question 77

Which structure is piretanide?

Answer: B

Explanation

Piretanide is a 5-sulfamoyl-3-aminobenzoic acid with a 4-phenoxy group and a pyrrolidine on the C3 nitrogen. It shows that a wide variety of substituents are tolerated on the amine in this series.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Bumetanide: n-butylamino at C3.
  • C: Furosemide: furfurylamino at C2 and Cl at C4.
  • D: Azosemide: tetrazole at C1.
Question 78

Identify this drug and its unique structural feature.

Answer: C

Explanation

A pyridine ring with a 4-(m-toluidino) group and SO₂–NH–CO–NH–isopropyl at C3 is torsemide, a 4-amino-3-pyridinesulfonylurea. The slide highlights the sulfonylurea moiety instead of a sulfonamide.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Bumetanide is a benzoic acid.
  • B: Metolazone has a bicyclic quinazolinone.
  • D: Chlorthalidone has an isoindolinone (phthalimidine).
Question 79

In the sulfonamide-diuretic pharmacophore figure, which drug is assigned to which chemical class?

Answer: A

Explanation

The figure branches the common pharmacophore (a primary sulfonamide next to an R group such as Cl, plus a carbonyl or sulfonyl group on the ring) into: carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (dichlorphenamide), thiazides (chlorothiazide), phthalimidines (chlorthalidone) and anthranilic acids (furosemide).

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Dichlorphenamide is the CA inhibitor (two sulfonamides).
  • C: Furosemide is the anthranilic acid.
  • D: Chlorothiazide is the thiazide.
Question 80

Which compound in the pharmacophore figure is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor?

Answer: D

Explanation

Dichlorphenamide is a dichlorobenzene carrying two SO₂NH₂ groups and no heterocycle or carboxylic acid. The figure labels it as the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Chlorothiazide: the thiazide (benzothiadiazine dioxide).
  • B: Chlorthalidone: the phthalimidine.
  • C: Furosemide: the anthranilic acid.
Question 81

For 5-sulfamoyl-2-aminobenzoic acids, which modification of furosemide is expected to abolish high-ceiling diuretic activity?

Answer: B

Explanation

The sulfamoyl group at position 5 is a prerequisite for optimal high-ceiling diuretic activity. The correct analog replaces SO₂NH₂ with Cl.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Azosemide: a tetrazole at C1 (still acidic) gives respectable activity.
  • C: Benzyl on the 2-amino group is one of the three substituents giving maximal activity.
  • D: Thienylmethyl is also among them.
Question 82

Rank these 2-amino substituents on 5-sulfamoyl-2-aminobenzoic acid from highest to lowest diuretic activity.

Answer: A

Explanation

Substitutions on the 2-amino group are limited. Only furfuryl, benzyl and thienylmethyl, in decreasing order, give derivatives with maximal diuretic activity. Furosemide carries the furfuryl group.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Furfuryl is first.
  • C: This reverses the order.
  • D: The lecture gives a ranking.
Question 83

How does azosemide differ structurally from furosemide, and is it still a potent diuretic?

Answer: D

Explanation

Azosemide has a tetrazole at position 1 and a thienylmethyl on the 2-amino group. The C1 substituent must be acidic; COOH is optimal, but a tetrazole can give respectable diuretic activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: The sulfamoyl group is present.
  • B: That describes bumetanide.
  • C: Torsemide has the sulfonylurea.
Question 84

Which statement about the 5-sulfamoyl-2-aminobenzoic acid SAR is correct?

Answer: C

Explanation

The 4-position activating group can be Cl or CF₃, and phenoxy, alkoxy, anilino or benzoyl are also possible.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Position 1 must be acidic.
  • B: 2-Amino substitutions are limited in this series. A wide variety is tolerated only in the 3-amino series.
  • D: Sulfamoyl at position 5 is a prerequisite.
Question 85

Bumetanide is about 50 times more potent than furosemide. Which structural variations explain this?

Answer: C

Explanation

Bumetanide has a 4-phenoxy group (electron-withdrawing, like Cl or CF₃) and its amine (n-butylamino) at position 3, not position 2 as in furosemide and azosemide. These variations account for the roughly 50-fold potency increase.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Bumetanide keeps the COOH.
  • B: Replacing the butyl with a furanylmethyl is not favorable.
  • D: That is torsemide.
Question 86

Which modification of bumetanide is expected to be unfavorable?

Answer: B

Explanation

Replacing the butyl on the C3 amine with a furanylmethyl group (as in furosemide) is not favorable. Replacing the 4-phenoxy with C₆H₅NH– or C₆H₅S– still gives favorable activity, and a wide variety of amine substituents, such as piretanide's pyrrolidine, is tolerated.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: 4-Phenylthio: favorable.
  • C: Piretanide: an active drug.
  • D: Bumetanide itself.
Question 87

Furosemide is metabolized to this compound. Name the reaction and its activity.

Answer: D

Explanation

The furfuryl group on the 2-amino nitrogen is removed, leaving a primary amine. This is N-dealkylation, and the product (4-chloro-5-sulfamoylanthranilic acid) is inactive. That fits the SAR, since only certain 2-amino substituents give maximal activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: No glucuronic acid is present, and the glucuronide is the active metabolite.
  • B: The sulfonamide is intact.
  • C: The furan has been removed, not oxidized.
Question 88

Which statement about furosemide metabolism is correct?

Answer: A

Explanation

About half of the furosemide load is excreted unchanged. N-Dealkylated furosemide is inactive. Furosemide glucuronide, formed at the carboxylic acid (an acyl glucuronide), is an active metabolite.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: About half is excreted unchanged.
  • C: This reverses the activities.
  • D: Furosemide has no OCH₃.
Question 89

Thiazides can form a water-soluble sodium salt. Which proton is removed first, and why?

Answer: B

Explanation

The hydrogen on N-2 is the most acidic because of the electron-withdrawing effect of the neighboring sulfone. The C-7 sulfonamide is an additional, but less acidic, site. These acidic protons allow formation of a water-soluble sodium salt.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: The 7-sulfonamide is less acidic than N-2.
  • C: The N-4 proton is not described as the acidic site.
  • D: Not acidic.
Question 90

Which thiazide analog is expected to be most active?

Answer: D

Explanation

An electron-withdrawing group is necessary at position 6. Cl or CF₃ gives highly active compounds, H gives little activity, and electron-releasing groups (CH₃, OCH₃) markedly reduce activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: 6-H: little diuretic activity.
  • B: 6-CH₃ (electron-releasing): markedly reduced.
  • C: 6-OCH₃ (electron-releasing): markedly reduced.
Question 91

Compared with its 6-chloro analog (HCTZ), what is expected of this 6-CF₃ thiazide?

Answer: A

Explanation

CF₃-substituted diuretics are more lipid-soluble and have a longer duration of action than their chloro analogs. Both are highly active electron-withdrawing groups.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: CF₃ is electron-withdrawing.
  • C: CF₃ compounds are highly active.
  • D: They are more lipid-soluble.
Question 92

What is expected of this compound, compared with hydrochlorothiazide?

Answer: C

Explanation

Replacing or removing the sulfonamide at position 7 yields compounds with little or no diuretic activity. Here the 7-SO₂NH₂ is absent.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: The essential 7-sulfonamide is missing.
  • B: Lipophilicity cannot make up for the missing pharmacophore.
  • D: No such conversion is described.
Question 93

Which structure is hydrochlorothiazide, and how does its potency compare with chlorothiazide?

Answer: D

Explanation

HCTZ is the 3,4-dihydro (saturated 3,4-bond) analog of chlorothiazide. Saturating this double bond gives a diuretic about 10-fold more active than the unsaturated parent.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Chlorothiazide: has the C3=N4 double bond.
  • B: Benzthiazide: unsaturated with a 3-benzylthiomethyl group.
  • C: An N-2-methylated HCTZ analog.
Question 94

Identify this drug and explain its pharmacokinetic advantage.

Answer: C

Explanation

A 3-(benzylthio)methyl group on the chlorothiazide skeleton is benzthiazide. Lipophilic substitution at position 3 (haloalkyl, aralkyl or thioether) markedly increases potency and gives a longer duration of action.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: HCTZ has no 3-substituent.
  • B: Metolazone has a bicyclic C=O and an N-aryl group.
  • D: Chlorthalidone is not a benzothiadiazine.
Question 95

A chemist methylates N-2 of hydrochlorothiazide. What is the predicted effect?

Answer: A

Explanation

Alkyl substitution on N-2 decreases polarity and increases the duration of diuretic action. Note that this also removes the most acidic proton.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: The lecture describes a longer duration, not a loss of activity.
  • C: Polarity decreases.
  • D: No such change is described.
Question 96

Identify this thiazide-like diuretic.

Answer: B

Explanation

A quinazolinone core (lactam C=O), a 2-methyl group, an N-3 ortho-tolyl, and Cl with SO₂NH₂ on the benzo ring. That is metolazone, which the lecture says is more potent than the thiazides.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Chlorthalidone has an isoindolinone (phthalimidine) with an OH.
  • C: Indapamide's structure is not drawn in this file.
  • D: Chlorothiazide has an SO₂ in the ring (benzothiadiazine dioxide).
Question 97

Why do chlorthalidone and metolazone share the mechanism of the thiazides even though they lack the benzothiadiazine ring?

Answer: D

Explanation

Thiazide-like diuretics lack the thiazide structure but keep the unsubstituted sulfonamide, so they share the thiazide mechanism. Chlorthalidone behaves pharmacologically like HCTZ, and metolazone is more potent than the thiazides.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Torsemide has the sulfonylurea.
  • B: Neither has a carboxylic acid.
  • C: Neither is a prodrug of HCTZ.

Coverage summary

Tested

  • ACE inhibitors: the general template (phenyl–(CH₂)ₙ, Zn²⁺ binder, X, N-ring), the three zinc binders, SH drawbacks, the essential N-ring COOH and its binding to the active site, phenylalanine/alanine/lysine mimicry, L-stereochemistry, large hydrophobic N-rings, prodrugs (all except captopril and lisinopril), structure ID of every drawn ACEI, and all four captopril metabolic routes.
  • ARBs and aliskiren: the general structure, acidic group options and what they mimic, the ortho requirement, tetrazole vs carboxylate, n-butyl as isoleucine, imidazole as histidine, valsartan's amide, benzimidazole replacements, ID of all four ARBs, aliskiren as a peptidomimetic renin inhibitor.
  • β-blockers: the isoprenaline → dichloroisoprenaline → pronethalol → propranolol sequence, the aryloxypropanolamine pharmacophore (OH and Asn, S-enantiomer, secondary amine, bulky R₁, R₂ lipophilicity, indole and ISA), linker replacements, side-chain substitution, heterocyclic replacements, lipophilicity and CNS effects, first/second/third generations, para hydrogen bonding for β₁ selectivity, ID of every drawn β-blocker, and propranolol and metoprolol metabolism.
  • CCBs: every 1,4-DHP SAR rule (C4 aryl, nonplanar alkyl, ring essential, N1, oxidation and reduction by CYP3A4, ortho/meta vs para, size not electronics, C3/C5 esters), the binding-pocket figure, DHP structure ID, verapamil requirements and metabolism, diltiazem metabolism and relative activity of metabolites.
  • Diuretics: the site-2/site-3 classification, the sulfonamide pharmacophore figure, 2-amino and 3-amino benzoic acid SAR, torsemide's sulfonylurea, furosemide metabolism, thiazide acidity and salt formation, positions 2, 3, 3–4, 6 and 7 of the thiazide SAR, and thiazide-like drugs.

Hard to convert, or tested lightly

  • Indapamide and chlorothiazide's use as a sodium salt are mentioned but indapamide's structure is not drawn, so it appears only as a distractor.
  • Propranolol hydroxylation at position 7 and the propranolol glucuronide are named but only 4′- and 5′-OH and DIP are drawn clearly, so the glucuronide was not given its own structure question.

Unclear points in the files

  • Metoprolol metabolism: the slide asks you to name the reactions but gives no answers. The names used here (α/benzylic hydroxylation, O-demethylation then oxidation, and loss of the isopropylamine with oxidation to an acid) come from reading the structures.
  • 3-aminobenzoic acid slide: it says a wide variety of substitutions is tolerated on the "2-amino group" of 5-sulfamoyl-3-aminobenzoic acid. From the drawings, this means the 3-amino group.
  • Telmisartan is drawn distorted on the ARB slide. The structure here is drawn from its standard connectivity.
  • Stereo labels: isoprenaline and pronethalol are labeled (R) while the aryloxypropanolamines are (S). This reflects the CIP naming change caused by the added oxygen, not an opposite 3D arrangement. Stereo wedges are left off the β-blocker drawings here, so stereochemistry is tested in words.
  • The direct renin inhibitor slide is repeated twice (slides 13 and 14).

Together these questions cover all three files, including every structure, SAR figure and metabolic scheme. All structures here were redrawn from the slides.
