Cholesterol and the statin pharmacophore

Cholesterol roles, HMG-CoA reductase step, mevastatin discovery, lactone prodrugs · 8 questions

Question 1

Which statement about cholesterol matches the lecture?

Answer: C

Explanation

Cholesterol is insoluble in aqueous medium. It is a structural component of every cell membrane and the starting material for steroid hormones, vitamin D and bile acids. It must be carried attached to protein, as lipoproteins.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: It is insoluble in water.
  • B: About 80% is made in the liver; the rest comes from the diet.
  • D: Bile acids come from cholesterol; bile pigments are not mentioned.
Question 2

In the biosynthesis scheme, which step does HMG-CoA reductase catalyze, and what is this product?

Answer: A

Explanation

HMG-CoA reductase reduces the thioester of HMG-CoA through an intermediate to mevalonic acid (a 3,5-dihydroxy acid: a tertiary 3-OH with a methyl, and a primary 5-OH). Mevalonic acid is then converted in several steps to cholesterol.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: This step comes before the reductase.
  • C: Several steps follow mevalonic acid.
  • D: Not shown in the scheme.
Question 3

Which statement about the discovery of statins is correct?

Answer: D

Explanation

HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (HMGRI) development began in 1976 with mevastatin (compactin), a fungal metabolite from two Penicillium species. It is a potent competitive inhibitor with 10,000-fold higher affinity than the substrate.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Mevastatin came first, in 1976.
  • B: It is a natural fungal metabolite.
  • C: Its affinity is 10,000-fold greater.
Question 4

Which grouping of natural and synthetic statins matches the lecture?

Answer: B

Explanation

The lecture lists mevastatin, lovastatin, pravastatin and simvastatin as natural statins (ring system A, decalin based) and atorvastatin and fluvastatin as synthetic statins.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: This reverses the classes.
  • C: Four are natural.
  • D: Not stated.
Question 5

Mevastatin and lovastatin are drawn with one structure. What is the only structural difference between them?

Answer: C

Explanation

On the shared structure, R = H gives mevastatin and R = CH₃ gives lovastatin. Both carry the 2-methylbutyrate ester and the lactone.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Both are lactones (prodrugs).
  • B: Neither has a fluorophenyl group.
  • D: Both have the ester side chain.
Question 6

Lovastatin as administered is shown. What must happen before it can inhibit HMG-CoA reductase?

Answer: A

Explanation

Lovastatin is an inactive prodrug lactone. In vivo hydrolysis opens it to the 3,5-dihydroxyacid moiety, which resembles the intermediate formed during HMG-CoA reduction (boxed on the slide). Compounds containing a lactone are prodrugs requiring in vivo hydrolysis.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: The lactone is inactive.
  • C: Not described.
  • D: Not the activation step.
Question 7

Which structure is the active form of lovastatin?

Answer: B

Explanation

The active form has the lactone opened into the 3,5-dihydroxyheptanoic acid (free COOH, 3-OH, 5-OH) while the decalin and 2-methylbutyrate ester are unchanged.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Lovastatin itself: the closed lactone prodrug.
  • C: Simvastatin: still a lactone, with an extra methyl on the ester side chain.
  • D: Mevastatin: a lactone lacking the ring methyl.
Question 8

Which part of the statin pharmacophore is described as essential for inhibitory activity?

Answer: D

Explanation

The 3,5-dihydroxycarboxylate (the 7-substituted-3,5-dihydroxyheptanoic acid) is essential for inhibition. It mimics the HMG-CoA reduction intermediate.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Its stereochemistry is not even important; changing it to an ether only decreases activity.
  • B: Important for ring B statins, but not called the essential pharmacophore.
  • C: Not described as essential.

Statin SAR, structures and metabolism

Dihydroxy acid rules, ring A and ring B SAR, structure ID, metabolites, atorvastatin binding · 23 questions

Question 9

Which analog is expected to be least active because it lacks an essential part of the pharmacophore?

Answer: B

Explanation

The correct structure has lost the 3-OH, so it no longer has the 3,5-dihydroxycarboxylate that is essential for inhibitory activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Atorvastatin itself: active.
  • C: para-Hydroxy atorvastatin: an equiactive metabolite.
  • D: ortho-Hydroxy atorvastatin: an equiactive metabolite.
Question 10

According to the SAR, how far must C5 of the dihydroxy acid be from the ring system, and what happens if this changes?

Answer: C

Explanation

A two-carbon distance between C5 and the ring system is essential. Changing it diminishes or fails to improve activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Not two carbons.
  • B: Not stated.
  • D: The distance is essential.
Question 11

Which atorvastatin analog keeps the correct linker length between C5 and the pyrrole ring?

Answer: D

Explanation

Atorvastatin has an ethyl (two-carbon) link between C5 and the pyrrole nitrogen. The ethyl group gives optimal activity for ring A compounds and some heterocycles such as the pyrrole of atorvastatin.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Three-carbon linker: the two-carbon distance is changed.
  • B: One-carbon linker: the distance is changed.
  • C: Correct linker, but the essential 3-OH is missing.
Question 12

Which pairing of the C6–C7 linker with the ring system is optimal, according to the SAR?

Answer: A

Explanation

A double bond between C6 and C7 can either increase or decrease activity depending on the ring. Ethyl is optimal for ring A and some heterocycles (pyrrole of atorvastatin). Ethenyl is optimal for ring B systems: indole (fluvastatin), quinoline (pitavastatin) and pyrimidine (rosuvastatin).

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: This reverses the pairing.
  • C: Ethenyl is not optimal for ring A or atorvastatin.
  • D: It can increase or decrease activity.
Question 13

Which stereochemical requirement applies to statins?

Answer: A

Explanation

The absolute stereochemistry of the 3- and 5-OH groups must match that of mevastatin and lovastatin.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Stereochemistry at C3 and C5 is required.
  • C: The ester side chain stereochemistry is not important.
  • D: Fluvastatin is a racemate of (3R,5S) and (3S,5R).
Question 14

Identify this statin.

Answer: B

Explanation

A decalin lactone with a 2,2-dimethylbutyrate ester: the extra methyl at R₂ on the ester side chain distinguishes simvastatin from lovastatin.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Lovastatin has 2-methylbutyrate (H at R₂).
  • C: Pravastatin is an open acid with a ring OH.
  • D: Mevastatin lacks the ring methyl and has 2-methylbutyrate.
Question 15

Why is simvastatin more potent than lovastatin, according to the ring A SAR?

Answer: C

Explanation

The only difference is an extra methyl at R₂ (2,2-dimethylbutyrate). The SAR states that methyl substitution at R₂ increases activity, so simvastatin is more potent than lovastatin.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Simvastatin is a lactone prodrug, like lovastatin.
  • B: Cyclohexane replacement would cause a 10,000-fold loss.
  • D: An ether would decrease activity.
Question 16

Which structure is pravastatin?

Answer: D

Explanation

Pravastatin is already an open 3,5-dihydroxy acid (not a prodrug) and has an OH at R₁ on the decalin in place of lovastatin's methyl. That hydroxyl enhances hydrophilicity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Lovastatin: lactone, methyl at R₁.
  • B: Simvastatin: lactone, extra ester methyl.
  • C: Lovastatin hydroxy acid: open acid but methyl, not OH, at R₁.
Question 17

Pravastatin differs from lovastatin's active form by a hydroxyl at R₁. What property does this change?

Answer: C

Explanation

Hydroxyl substitution at R₁ enhances hydrophilicity, which is why pravastatin is a more hydrophilic statin.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Pravastatin is given as the active open acid.
  • B: The OH makes it more hydrophilic.
  • D: The decalin ring does the anchoring.
Question 18

Which modification of a ring A statin causes the largest loss of activity?

Answer: B

Explanation

The decalin ring is essential for anchoring the compound in the enzyme active site. Replacing it with a cyclohexane caused a 10,000-fold decrease in activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Simvastatin: more potent.
  • C: Ester converted to ether: activity decreases, but much less than losing the decalin.
  • D: Pravastatin: active, more hydrophilic.
Question 19

A chemist converts lovastatin's 2-methylbutyrate ester into the corresponding ether, and separately inverts the stereocenter of the ester side chain. What does the SAR predict?

Answer: D

Explanation

Stereochemistry of the ester side chain is not important for activity, but converting the ester to an ether decreases activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Only the ether change reduces activity.
  • B: It decreases activity.
  • C: Side chain stereochemistry is not important.
Question 20

Identify this statin.

Answer: A

Explanation

A pyrrole core carrying a para-fluorophenyl, a phenyl, an isopropyl and a phenylcarboxamide (anilide), linked to the dihydroxy acid by an ethyl chain. That is atorvastatin.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Fluvastatin has an indole and an ethenyl link.
  • C: Rosuvastatin has a pyrimidine with an N-methyl methanesulfonamide.
  • D: Pitavastatin has a quinoline with a cyclopropyl.
Question 21

Which structure is rosuvastatin?

Answer: B

Explanation

Rosuvastatin has a pyrimidine ring bearing a para-fluorophenyl, an isopropyl and an N-methyl methanesulfonamide, with an ethenyl link to the dihydroxy acid.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Pitavastatin: quinoline with cyclopropyl.
  • C: N-desmethyl rosuvastatin: the metabolite, N–H instead of N–CH₃.
  • D: Fluvastatin: indole.
Question 22

Identify this statin.

Answer: D

Explanation

A quinoline core with a cyclopropyl group and a para-fluorophenyl, joined by an ethenyl to the dihydroxy acid. That is pitavastatin.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Fluvastatin has an N-isopropyl indole.
  • B: Rosuvastatin has a pyrimidine.
  • C: Atorvastatin has a pyrrole and an ethyl link.
Question 23

In the ring B general structure, which statement is correct?

Answer: A

Explanation

All these points are on the ring B SAR slide: non-coplanarity of the fluorophenyl, W/X/Y/Z as C or N, and n = 0 or 1.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Coplanarity causes loss of activity.
  • C: They can be carbon or nitrogen.
  • D: Five-membered rings (n = 0) also work, as in atorvastatin's pyrrole.
Question 24

In ring B statins, substitution at the R position with aryl groups, hydrocarbon chains, amides or sulfonamides has what effect? Which two drugs show this?

Answer: C

Explanation

R substitution with aryl groups, hydrocarbon chains, amides or sulfonamides enhances lipophilicity and inhibitory activity. Atorvastatin carries an amide (anilide) and rosuvastatin a sulfonamide at this position.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: It enhances lipophilicity.
  • B: It enhances activity.
  • D: Neither is a prodrug.
Question 25

This metabolite of atorvastatin is shown. What is its activity?

Answer: B

Explanation

The anilide ring has been hydroxylated. Atorvastatin's ortho- and para-hydroxylated metabolites are equiactive with the parent and contribute significantly to its overall activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: They are active.
  • C: This describes N-desmethyl rosuvastatin.
  • D: Not stated.
Question 26

Rosuvastatin is metabolized to a limited extent to this compound. Name the reaction and its activity.

Answer: D

Explanation

The sulfonamide nitrogen has lost its methyl (N–CH₃ → N–H). N-desmethyl rosuvastatin can contribute to activity but is seven-fold less potent.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Equiactive hydroxylated metabolites belong to atorvastatin.
  • B: No lactone is formed.
  • C: No glucuronide is shown.
Question 27

Which statement about statin metabolites matches the lecture?

Answer: A

Explanation

Fluvastatin's active hydroxy metabolites stay local and do not contribute. Pravastatin's oxidative metabolites have minimal, insignificant activity. Atorvastatin's ortho/para-hydroxy metabolites are equiactive.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: They do not circulate systemically.
  • C: Pravastatin metabolites have minimal activity.
  • D: They are equiactive.
Question 28

Which structure is fluvastatin?

Answer: C

Explanation

Fluvastatin has an N-isopropyl indole with a para-fluorophenyl at C3 and an ethenyl link to the 3,5-dihydroxy acid.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Des-isopropyl fluvastatin: indole N–H (metabolite).
  • B: Pitavastatin: quinoline with cyclopropyl.
  • D: 5-Hydroxy fluvastatin: OH on the indole benzene ring (metabolite).
Question 29

Fluvastatin is converted by CYP to this product. Name the metabolite.

Answer: D

Explanation

The indole nitrogen has lost its isopropyl group and now carries N–H. In the metabolism scheme this is des-isopropyl fluvastatin. The other CYP products are 5- and 6-hydroxy fluvastatin and a product hydroxylated on both the indole ring and the isopropyl group.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: 5-Hydroxy keeps the isopropyl and adds a ring OH.
  • B: 6-Hydroxy keeps the isopropyl and adds a ring OH.
  • C: Fluvastatin has no N-methyl.
Question 30

Which statement about fluvastatin is correct?

Answer: A

Explanation

All points are on the fluvastatin slide. It is classed as a synthetic statin and is drawn as the open acid.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: It is a racemate and relatively hydrophilic.
  • C: It is synthetic.
  • D: It is given as the open acid.
Question 31

In the binding figure of atorvastatin in HMG-CoA reductase, which interaction is correctly paired?

Answer: B

Explanation

The figure shows an ion-dipole bond between the partially negative F and the positive guanidinium of Arg-590, a hydrogen bond from Ser-565 OH to the amide carbonyl, and van der Waals contacts between the isopropyl group and Leu, Val and Ala.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: These are swapped.
  • C: The amide C=O is hydrogen-bonded to Ser-565.
  • D: No covalent bonds are shown.

Ezetimibe and fibrates

β-Lactam and NPC1L1, phenoxyisobutyric acid SAR, prodrug esters, fenofibrate metabolism · 13 questions

Question 32

Identify this drug and the group that binds its target.

Answer: C

Explanation

A four-membered β-lactam ring with two para-fluorophenyl groups, a para-hydroxyphenyl and a benzylic OH is ezetimibe. The slide states that the β-lactam binds the Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) protein responsible for cholesterol absorption.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Ezetimibe does not inhibit HMG-CoA reductase.
  • B: Probucol is a bisphenol thioether.
  • D: This is not atorvastatin.
Question 33

Which statement about ezetimibe's actions is correct?

Answer: A

Explanation

Ezetimibe binds a transport protein in the small intestinal wall, lowering cholesterol in chylomicrons. It is selective and does not interfere with TG, lipid-soluble vitamin or nutrient absorption. LDL falls by up to 20%.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: It is selective for cholesterol.
  • C: It does not inhibit synthesis; the liver actually increases synthesis in response.
  • D: It lowers LDL.
Question 34

A patient on ezetimibe alone has only a modest LDL drop. Why does the lecture say ezetimibe–statin combinations are particularly effective?

Answer: C

Explanation

The liver compensates for reduced cholesterol absorption by increasing de novo synthesis. Combining ezetimibe with a statin blocks both absorption and synthesis.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: None of these is described.
  • B: None of these is described.
  • D: None of these is described.
Question 35

Which statement about fibrate mechanisms in the lecture is correct?

Answer: D

Explanation

Fibrates induce lipoprotein lipase (lowering VLDL) and stimulate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPAR), which increases apo AI and AII production and raises HDL.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: That is statins.
  • B: That is resins.
  • C: That is ezetimibe.
Question 36

Fibrates are analogs of which parent structure, and which group is essential for activity?

Answer: B

Explanation

The general fibrate structure is aromatic ring–O–(spacer)–C(CH₃)₂–COOH. Fibrates are analogs of phenoxyisobutyric acid, and the isobutyric acid group is essential for activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: The gem-dimethyl (isobutyric) part is required.
  • C: Niacin is a separate agent.
  • D: Not the parent structure.
Question 37

Which compound is expected to have fibrate activity, according to the SAR?

Answer: D

Explanation

Clofibric acid has the intact isobutyric acid group (two methyls on the carbon next to COOH) linked through oxygen to a para-chlorophenyl. The isobutyric acid group is essential for activity.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Phenoxyacetic acid: no methyls, so no isobutyric acid group.
  • B: Only one methyl: not an isobutyric acid.
  • C: Niacin is not a fibrate.
Question 38

Identify this fibrate and its status.

Answer: B

Explanation

The para-chlorophenoxyisobutyric acid ethyl ester is clofibrate. Esterified fibrates (clofibrate, fenofibrate) must be hydrolyzed to the carboxylic acid (clofibric acid) to be active.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Clofibric acid has a free COOH.
  • C: Fenofibrate has a benzophenone and an isopropyl ester.
  • D: Ciprofibrate has a dichlorocyclopropyl group and a free acid.
Question 39

Which structure is fenofibrate?

Answer: A

Explanation

Fenofibrate has a para-chlorobenzophenone attached through oxygen to the isobutyric acid, which is esterified as the isopropyl ester (prodrug).

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Fenofibric acid: the free acid (active form).
  • C: Clofibrate: single chlorophenyl ring and ethyl ester.
  • D: Benzhydrol fenofibric acid: the ketone reduced to an alcohol.
Question 40

Identify this drug and explain why it is active even though it is not a phenoxyisobutyric acid.

Answer: C

Explanation

A 2,5-dimethylphenoxy group linked by a three-carbon (n-propyl) spacer to C(CH₃)₂COOH is gemfibrozil. Most fibrates are phenoxyisobutyric acids, but adding an n-propyl spacer, as in gemfibrozil, still results in an active drug.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Not clofibrate.
  • B: Not ciprofibrate.
  • D: Gemfibrozil keeps the isobutyric acid.
Question 41

Which structural feature gives ciprofibrate a significantly longer half-life?

Answer: B

Explanation

Para substitution with a chloro group or a chlorine-containing cyclopropyl ring produces compounds with significantly longer half-lives. Ciprofibrate has a 2,2-dichlorocyclopropyl at the para position.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: The spacer belongs to gemfibrozil.
  • C: Ciprofibrate is a free acid.
  • D: That is fenofibrate.
Question 42

Identify this compound.

Answer: A

Explanation

Clofibric acid is linked as an ester through –O–CH₂CH₂–O– to nicotinic acid (pyridine-3-carboxylic acid). The lecture describes etofibrate as a fibrate produced by combining a clofibrate ester linked to niacin.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: Fenofibrate has a benzophenone.
  • C: Clofibrate is a simple ethyl ester.
  • D: Nicotinamide is a simple amide.
Question 43

Fenofibrate is converted to this metabolite. Which reaction produced it?

Answer: C

Explanation

The benzophenone C=O has become CH–OH. In the metabolism scheme, reduction gives benzhydrol fenofibric acid (the ester is also cleaved to the free acid in the drawn product).

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Hydrolysis only removes the isopropyl group, giving fenofibric acid.
  • B: Glucuronidation attaches glucuronic acid to the COOH.
  • D: There is no N to dealkylate.
Question 44

In fenofibrate metabolism, which sequence leads to the glucuronide?

Answer: D

Explanation

Fenofibrate → (hydrolysis) fenofibric acid → (glucuronidation) fenofibric acid glucuronide (an ester at the COOH).

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Reduction is a separate branch.
  • B: Not shown.
  • C: The free acid is needed for glucuronidation.

Bile acid sequestrants, niacin and probucol

Resin chemistry, charge and binding, nicotinic acid vs nicotinamide, HCAR2, probucol · 10 questions

Question 45

Which statement describes bile acid sequestrants correctly?

Answer: C

Explanation

All points in option B are listed. Cholestyramine and similar polymers adsorb bile acids through a combination of electrostatic and hydrophobic forces. They are taken as a slurry or gel.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: They are not absorbed.
  • B: They exchange anions.
  • D: They are inert to digestive enzymes.
Question 46

Cholic acid (shown) binds to cholestyramine. What forces hold it to the resin?

Answer: D

Explanation

The slide states that cholestyramine and similar polymers adsorb bile acids through a combination of electrostatic and hydrophobic forces. The figure shows the carboxylate of cholic acid next to the N⁺ of the resin.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Not described.
  • B: Not described.
  • C: Not described.
Question 47

What is the chemical composition of cholestyramine?

Answer: A

Explanation

Cholestyramine is made from styrene and divinylbenzene (the cross-linker) and carries CH₂N⁺(CH₃)₃ (trimethylbenzylammonium) groups with chloride counter-ions.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: That is colestipol.
  • C: Not described.
  • D: Not described.
Question 48

Which pair are the precursors of colestipol?

Answer: B

Explanation

Colestipol is a copolymer of tetraethylenepentamine and 1-chloro-2,3-epoxypropane (epichlorohydrin), supplied as a hygroscopic powder. In the polymer, R = H or an epichlorohydrin cross-link.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: These make cholestyramine.
  • C: These relate to etofibrate.
  • D: These relate to etofibrate.
Question 49

How do the three resins differ in how they become positively charged?

Answer: D

Explanation

Cholestyramine (quaternary ammonium) and colesevelam are positively charged; colestipol (made of secondary and tertiary amines) becomes positively charged in the small intestine to bind negatively charged bile acids.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: They carry positive charges.
  • B: This reverses them.
  • C: Not stated.
Question 50

Which structure is niacin?

Answer: B

Explanation

Niacin is pyridine-3-carboxylic acid (nicotinic acid): the COOH is at position 3 relative to the ring nitrogen.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Nicotinamide: the amide form.
  • C: Pyridine-4-carboxylic acid (isonicotinic acid): wrong position.
  • D: Clofibric acid: a fibrate.
Question 51

A patient needs niacin supplementation to prevent pellagra but cannot tolerate flushing. Based on the structure–effect note, which form is used and why?

Answer: A

Explanation

The carboxylic group of niacin is important for its lipid-modifying effects but also causes flushing. Nicotinamide (the amide) does not cause flushing and is used for nutritional supplementation to prevent pellagra. It is therefore not used for its lipid effects.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B: The acid causes flushing.
  • C: Not supplements for pellagra.
  • D: Not supplements for pellagra.
Question 52

How does nicotinic acid reduce the release of free fatty acids from adipose tissue?

Answer: C

Explanation

Nicotinic acid activates HCAR2, a G-protein-coupled receptor found in adipose tissue and immune cells. Binding inhibits lipase in adipose tissue and reduces free fatty acid release.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: That is statins.
  • B: That is fibrates.
  • D: That is resins.
Question 53

Identify this drug.

Answer: D

Explanation

Two phenol rings, each flanked by two bulky tert-butyl groups, joined through two thioether sulfurs on a gem-dimethyl carbon. That is probucol.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: Ezetimibe has a β-lactam.
  • B: Gemfibrozil has an isobutyric acid.
  • C: Etofibrate has a pyridine ester.
Question 54

Which pairing of a structural feature of probucol with its role is correct?

Answer: C

Explanation

Probucol is a bisphenol with two thioether bridges. Its phenols give antioxidant activity, the tert-butyl groups increase lipophilicity for incorporation into LDL, and the sulfur bridges add to its antioxidant and CV effects. It was withdrawn in Western countries over cardiac safety concerns but is still used in some Asian countries.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A: They increase lipophilicity.
  • B: Not stated.
  • D: That is ezetimibe's β-lactam.

Coverage summary

Tested

  • Cholesterol and biosynthesis: functions, insolubility, the HMG-CoA → mevalonic acid step, 80% hepatic synthesis.
  • Statin discovery and classes: mevastatin (compactin), fungal origin, 10,000-fold affinity, natural vs synthetic, mevastatin vs lovastatin.
  • Pharmacophore and SAR: lactone prodrug activation, essential 3,5-dihydroxycarboxylate, C3/C5 stereochemistry, two-carbon C5–ring distance, ethyl vs ethenyl by ring type, R₂ methyl (simvastatin), R₁ OH (pravastatin), decalin anchoring and cyclohexane loss, ester vs ether, ring B coplanarity, W/X/Y/Z and n, lipophilic R groups.
  • Structure ID: lovastatin, its acid, simvastatin, pravastatin, atorvastatin, fluvastatin, pitavastatin, rosuvastatin, ezetimibe, clofibrate, fenofibrate, gemfibrozil, ciprofibrate, etofibrate, niacin, nicotinamide, probucol.
  • Metabolism: equiactive hydroxy-atorvastatin, N-desmethyl rosuvastatin (7-fold weaker), fluvastatin CYP products, pravastatin, fenofibrate hydrolysis, reduction and glucuronidation.
  • Binding: atorvastatin with Arg-590, Ser-565 and Leu/Val/Ala.
  • Other agents: ezetimibe β-lactam, selectivity and statin synergy; fibrate mechanism and SAR; resin chemistry and charge; niacin COOH, HCAR2, nicotinamide; probucol features.

Notes on the file

  • Colesevelam is named but not drawn, so it is tested only in words.
  • The fluvastatin metabolite hydroxylated on both the indole ring and the isopropyl group is shown without a name, so it was not given its own question.
  • Fluvastatin, pitavastatin and rosuvastatin are drawn here without stereo wedges at C3 and C5; stereochemistry is tested in words.
  • Pitavastatin and rosuvastatin are not placed in the natural or synthetic list on the slide.
  • All structures were redrawn from the slides.

These questions cover all 23 slides, including every structure, SAR figure and metabolic scheme. They are separate from the Hypertension bank.
